content: The 2015-16 influenza vaccination recommendations from the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) include several updates compared to the 2014 guidelines. These updates address the antigenic composition of the vaccines, the available vaccine products, dosing algorithms for children aged 6 months through 8 years, and the use of live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) versus inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV). The preferential recommendation for LAIV in healthy children aged 2 through 8 years, which was present in the 2014-15 guidelines, has been removed due to new data on vaccine effectiveness. Influenza Vaccine Composition for 2015-16 For the 2015-16 season, trivalent influenza vaccines in the United States will include hemagglutinin (HA) components derived from the following strains: 1. A/California/7/2009 (H1N1)-like virus. 2. A/Switzerland/9715293/2013 (H3N2)-like virus. 3. B/Phuket/3073/2013-like virus (Yamagata lineage). Quadrivalent vaccines will include the above three strains and an additional B/Brisbane/60/2008-like virus (Victoria lineage). This represents changes in the H3N2 and B virus components compared to the 2014-15 season. Vaccine Products and Indications Multiple influenza vaccine products are expected to be available for the 2015-16 season. These include both trivalent and quadrivalent formulations, as well as vaccines designed for specific populations, such as high-dose vaccines for older adults. ACIP does not express a preference for any specific vaccine product when multiple options are available for a given individual. Providers should consult the FDA-approved prescribing information for detailed guidance on indications, contraindications, and precautions. Dosing for Children Aged 6 Months Through 8 Years Children in this age group who are receiving the influenza vaccine for the first time, or who have not previously received at least two doses of influenza vaccine before July 1, 2015, require two doses of the vaccine. These doses should be administered at least four weeks apart. For children who have previously received two or more doses, only one dose is required for the 2015-16 season. Studies suggest that longer intervals between the two doses do not compromise the immune response. Use of LAIV and IIV Both LAIV and IIV have been shown to be effective in children and adults. However, recent data indicate that LAIV did not perform as well as expected against the influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 virus during the 2013-14 season. As a result, ACIP no longer recommends a preference for LAIV over IIV in healthy children aged 2 through 8 years. For individuals with chronic medical conditions, data comparing the safety and efficacy of LAIV and IIV are limited. In general, LAIV is not recommended for individuals with asthma, recent wheezing, or other underlying medical conditions that increase the risk of complications from influenza. Influenza Vaccination for Persons with Egg Allergy Most influenza vaccines are produced using egg-based methods, which may raise concerns for individuals with egg allergies. However, studies have shown that severe allergic reactions to egg-based influenza vaccines are rare. For individuals with a history of severe egg allergy, vaccination should be performed in a medical setting equipped to manage anaphylaxis. Recombinant influenza vaccine (RIV3), which is egg-free, is an option for individuals aged 18 years and older. For children with egg allergy, data suggest that both IIV and LAIV are generally well-tolerated, but vaccination should be performed under appropriate medical supervision. Timing of Vaccination Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for all individuals aged 6 months and older who do not have contraindications. Vaccination should ideally occur before the onset of influenza activity in the community, with October being the optimal time for administration. However, vaccination should continue to be offered as long as influenza viruses are circulating. For children requiring two doses, the first dose should be administered as soon as the vaccine becomes available, with the second dose given at least four weeks later. Vaccination for Immunocompromised Individuals Live attenuated influenza vaccines (LAIV) are generally contraindicated for individuals with immunocompromising conditions. Inactivated influenza vaccines (IIV) are preferred for these populations. The Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) provides detailed guidance on vaccine selection and timing for individuals with specific immunocompromising conditions, such as those undergoing organ transplantation or receiving immunosuppressive therapy. Summary of Key Considerations The 2015-16 influenza vaccines include updated strains to match circulating viruses. Children aged 6 months through 8 years may require two doses of the vaccine, depending on their vaccination history. LAIV is no longer preferentially recommended for healthy children aged 2 through 8 years. Individuals with egg allergy can generally receive influenza vaccines safely, but precautions may be necessary for those with severe allergies. Immunocompromised individuals should receive IIV rather than LAIV. These recommendations aim to optimize protection against influenza while addressing specific needs and considerations for different populations.
